This report contrasts vocabulary growth in children with **Down syndrome (DS)**
against **typically developing (TD)** children, using the fitted PyMC models.
Every contrast is a **per-draw difference of the disjoint DS and TD posteriors**:
because the two datasets share no studies or children, the joint posterior
factorises, so pairing draws gives an _exact_ credible interval for any contrast
with **no joint model** required. (The generative joint model that would make the
DS–TD gap itself a parameter is not built and holds no reserved model number —
it was reserved as VG16 until that number was taken by the Down syndrome
within-child cross-lag — and this report shows the headline questions are already
answerable without it. The full reasoning, including what such a model could
share across the two populations and what would reopen the decision, is in
`notes/202608200906-joint-ds-td-model-not-built.md`.)

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd


def _nearest(df, col, val):
    return df.iloc[(df[col] - val).abs().argmin()]


def _hdi(m, lo, hi, dec=0):
    if pd.isna(m):
        return "—"
    return f"{m:.{dec}f} [{lo:.{dec}f}, {hi:.{dec}f}]"


def band_at(df, idxcol, idxval, prefix, dec=0, cov_col=None, cov_min=0.80):
    """Format 'median [ci_lo, ci_hi]' for `prefix` at the row nearest idxval."""
    r = _nearest(df, idxcol, idxval)
    if cov_col is not None and float(r.get(cov_col, 1.0)) < cov_min:
        return "—"
    m = r[f"{prefix}_median"]
    return _hdi(m, r[f"{prefix}_ci_lo"], r[f"{prefix}_ci_hi"], dec)


def plain_at(df, idxcol, idxval, dec=0, cov_min=0.80):
    """Format 'median [ci_lo, ci_hi]' for a single unprefixed series."""
    r = _nearest(df, idxcol, idxval)
    if "coverage" in df.columns and float(r.get("coverage", 1.0)) < cov_min:
        return "—"
    return _hdi(r["median"], r["ci_lo"], r["ci_hi"], dec)
```

## Method and scope

| Role                                   | Model(s)                          |
| -------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| DS expected words / ratio / delay      | **VG20** (joint U+S, study+subject REs, correlated) |
| DS dispersion / distribution           | **VG20** (as above)                     |
| DS between-child heterogeneity         | **VG20** (as above)                     |
| DS sign-inclusive total expressive     | **VG15** (joint sign/speech, `p_any`)   |
| TD spoken / understood (univariate)    | **VG11 / VG12** (study RE)              |
| TD joint (comprehension-matched)       | **VG13** (joint, 8–18 mo)               |

All contrasts are at the **population level** (random effects excluded, so the
estimand is identical on both sides) and restricted to the **empirical age/level
overlap**.

Every DS row now comes from the same model. It did not always: dispersion and
distributional contrasts used the **study-RE-only** VG07, because κ only means the
same thing on both sides when the two sides agree on whether a subject random
effect is present to absorb between-child variance, and VG11/VG12 were study-RE
only. Adding child random effects to the TD models (#164) inverted that — VG07's κ
now carries child variance the TD models' κ does not — so the dispersion key moved
to the DS model of record on **2026-08-05**. This table went on naming VG07 until
**2026-08-19**, when the same edit that moved the model of record to VG20 caught
it; readers of the earlier editions were told the dispersion contrast came from a
model it had not come from for two weeks. The numbers in those editions were
computed from VG10 and are unaffected.

::: {.callout-important}
**The TD models only span ~8–30 months.** Several estimands are therefore
identified only at younger ages or lower vocabulary levels. Each table cell is
blanked (—) where posterior **coverage** of the comparable region falls below
0.80; read the supported range only.
:::

## The gap is large and production-specific

```{python}
ew_s = pd.read_csv("ds_td_spoken_re_expected_words.csv")
ew_u = pd.read_csv("ds_td_understood_re_expected_words.csv")

ages = [12, 18, 24, 30]
rows = []
for a in ages:
    ru, rs = _nearest(ew_u, "age_months", a), _nearest(ew_s, "age_months", a)
    rows.append({
        "Age (mo)": a,
        "Understood TD": f"{ru['TD_median']:.0f}",
        "Understood DS": f"{ru['DS_median']:.0f}",
        "Understood ×": f"{ru['ratio_median']:.1f}",
        "Spoken TD": f"{rs['TD_median']:.0f}",
        "Spoken DS": f"{rs['DS_median']:.0f}",
        "Spoken ×": f"{rs['ratio_median']:.0f}",
    })
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Age (mo)")
```

Expected vocabulary (latent mean out of the 810-word reference inventory). The
comprehension gap is large (~4× at 24 mo) but the **production** gap is far larger
(tens-fold), and P(TD > DS) = 1.00 across the supported overlap on both outcomes.

![Expected words understood — TD vs DS](ds_td_understood_re_expected_words.png){#fig-ew-u .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![Expected words spoken — TD vs DS](ds_td_spoken_re_expected_words.png){#fig-ew-s .lightbox fig-align="left"}

## A developmental stretch, not a constant shift

```{python}
ad_s = pd.read_csv("ds_td_spoken_re_attainment_delay.csv")
ad_u = pd.read_csv("ds_td_understood_re_attainment_delay.csv")

levels = [10, 50, 100, 200, 300]
rows = []
for v in levels:
    rows.append({
        "Level v (words)": v,
        "Understood delay (mo)": plain_at(ad_u, "words", v, dec=0),
        "Spoken delay (mo)": plain_at(ad_s, "words", v, dec=0),
    })
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Level v (words)")
```

The attainment delay $D(v)$ — months DS reaches level $v$ after TD — **grows with
the level** on both outcomes. A flat $D(v)$ would mean a pure time-shift; the
rising curve means the gap _widens_ with development, and production lags
comprehension at every level.

![Attainment delay D(v) — understood](ds_td_understood_re_attainment_delay.png){#fig-ad-u .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![Attainment delay D(v) — spoken](ds_td_spoken_re_attainment_delay.png){#fig-ad-s .lightbox fig-align="left"}

### Peak learning-rate age

```{python}
pk = pd.read_csv("ds_td_peak_growth_age.csv").set_index("outcome")
rows = []
for outcome in ("understood", "spoken"):
    r = pk.loc[outcome]
    rows.append({
        "Outcome": outcome,
        "DS peak (mo)": f"{r['peak_age_DS_median']:.0f} "
                        f"[{r['peak_age_DS_ci_lo']:.0f}, {r['peak_age_DS_ci_hi']:.0f}]",
        "DS censored": f"{r['peak_age_DS_boundary_frac']:.0%}",
        "TD peak (mo)": f"{r['peak_age_TD_median']:.0f} "
                        f"[{r['peak_age_TD_ci_lo']:.0f}, {r['peak_age_TD_ci_hi']:.0f}]",
    })
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Outcome")
```

DS peak-velocity age arrives several years after TD on both outcomes — a stretch,
not a shift.

::: {.callout-warning title="Peak-growth age is right-censored for DS"}
The DS peak ages are **boundary-censored**: the upper HDI sits at the 115-month
edge of the search grid, and a non-trivial fraction of posterior draws (≈12%
spoken, ≈7% understood) place the peak _at_ that boundary — i.e. for those draws
the DS trajectory has not clearly peaked within the supported age range. The
**direction** (DS peaks much later than TD) is robust; the specific DS figure and
its upper interval are only weakly identified and should be read as a lower
bound. TD peaks (≈18 mo understood, ≈23 mo spoken) are cleanly identified
(< 0.1% censored).
:::

## Expressive-specific delay

DS production is delayed _beyond_ what its comprehension delay alone predicts,
shown two complementary ways.

### Level-indexed — at matched vocabulary size

```{python}
xd = pd.read_csv("ds_td_expressive_delay.csv")
rows = []
for N in [50]:
    r = _nearest(xd, "words", N)
    val = band_at(xd, "words", N, "dexp", dec=1, cov_col="dexp_coverage")
    rows.append({
        "Vocabulary N (words)": N,
        "Δ_exp (extra months to say)": val,
        "P(Δ_exp > 0)": f"{r['dexp_p_gt0']:.2f}" if val != "—" else "—",
    })
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Vocabulary N (words)")
```

$\Delta_{exp}(N)$ = (spoken attainment delay) − (understood attainment delay): at
a matched vocabulary _size_, the extra months DS takes to **say** the words it
**understands**, relative to TD. The window where both populations reach N within
support is narrow — TD (VG13, 8–18 mo) already understands ~40 words at its
youngest supported age, and DS spoken-delay coverage thins above ~75 — so it is
robustly identified around **N ≈ 50: ≈12.5 months [9.7, 15.3], P > 0 = 1.00**.
DS takes about a year longer to say the words it understands, at matched
vocabulary size. The figure below shows the two component delays — months DS is
behind TD to **say** N words (green, identified at low N) and to **understand** N
words (blue, identified at high N). They overlap only near N ≈ 50, which is why
Δ_exp is reported as a single-level estimate rather than a curve.

![Attainment delay: comprehension (blue) vs production (green)](ds_td_expressive_attainment_delay.png){#fig-dexp-attain .lightbox fig-align="left"}

### Age-indexed — comprehension-equivalent developmental age

```{python}
ca = pd.read_csv("ds_td_expressive_equivalent_age.csv")
rows = []
for a in [24, 36]:
    r = _nearest(ca, "age_months", a)
    rows.append({
        "DS age (mo)": a,
        "Extra expressive delay (mo)": band_at(
            ca, "age_months", a, "dexpAge", dec=1, cov_col="dexpAge_coverage"),
        "P(> 0)": f"{r['dexpAge_p_gt0']:.2f}" if not pd.isna(r['dexpAge_p_gt0']) else "—",
    })
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("DS age (mo)")
```

The extra-expressive delay at a fixed _age_ (comprehension-equivalent minus
production-equivalent TD age) is smaller and fades by ~48 mo — because at a fixed
age DS comprehension is _also_ heavily delayed, so both map to early-TD ages and
the _extra_ lag compresses. The level-indexed Δ_exp above is the cleaner statistic.

![DS developmental-equivalent TD age](ds_td_expressive_equivalent_age.png){#fig-cea .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![Receptive vs expressive delay, and the extra expressive gap](ds_td_expressive_delay_by_age.png){#fig-cea-delay .lightbox fig-align="left"}

### Comprehension-matched production ratio

```{python}
qu = pd.read_csv("ds_td_comprehension_q_at_U.csv")
rows = []
for N in [50, 100, 150]:
    r = _nearest(qu, "words", N)
    rows.append({
        "Understood N (words)": N,
        "q TD": band_at(qu, "words", N, "q_TD", dec=2, cov_col="dq_coverage"),
        "q DS": band_at(qu, "words", N, "q_DS", dec=2, cov_col="dq_coverage"),
        "Δq (TD−DS)": band_at(qu, "words", N, "dq", dec=2, cov_col="dq_coverage"),
        "P(Δq>0)": f"{r['dq_p_gt0']:.2f}",
    })
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Understood N (words)")
```

At equal comprehension, DS speaks a smaller fraction of the words it understands
(Δq > 0, P ≈ 1.00 from N ≈ 50 to ≈ 150, converging by N ≈ 200). The TD comparator
(VG13, 8–18 mo) already understands ~40 words at its youngest supported age, so q
is **not identified below N ≈ 50 for TD** — those points are dropped by the
coverage filter, and the curves begin where both populations genuinely reach that
comprehension level within support.

![Production ratio at matched comprehension q(U=N)](ds_td_comprehension_q_at_U.png){#fig-qatu .lightbox fig-align="left"}

Fraction of DS children at or below the **TD 10th centile** word count. By age 2,

## Between-child variability

Beyond the mean, how does the _spread_ between children compare? Both comparators
carry study **and** child random effects, which splits the question in two, and the
halves have to be read separately:

- **Between-child heterogeneity** — how far children of the same age sit from one
  another — lives in the subject random-effect scale $\tau$. This is the quantity
  that answers "are children in this population more alike?", and it is reported in
  @sec-between-child below.
- **Residual dispersion** — what the Beta-Binomial layer still has to absorb once
  the study and child effects have taken their share — lives in $\kappa$ and the
  quantities derived from it, $\sigma_Y$ and $\varphi$. That is this section.

Treating the second as if it were the first is the standard trap here, and in the
TD models it is a specific one: $\tau_{subject}$ and $\kappa$ are an explicit
reparameterisation of a *single* logit-scale scatter budget (see
`models.gp_utils.build_variance_partition`), so reading either alone silently
attributes the whole budget to whichever half is in view.

Two derived quantities: the implied per-child word-count SD $\sigma_Y$ (absolute
spread, which scales with the mean) and the overdispersion factor $\varphi =
(\kappa + n)/(\kappa + 1)$, the variance inflation over a Binomial at the same
mean. $\varphi$ removes the explicit $p(1-p)$ term that $\sigma_Y$ carries, but it
is **not** mean-independent: $\kappa$ is itself level-driven in this family, so a
cross-population contrast still carries part of the difference in where the two
populations sit. A ratio $\varphi_{TD}/\varphi_{DS} > 1$ means TD counts are the
more overdispersed *given the model's fitted means*, not that TD children vary
more.

```{python}
ds_s = pd.read_csv("ds_td_spoken_re_dispersion.csv")
ds_u = pd.read_csv("ds_td_understood_re_dispersion.csv")
rows = []
for a in [8, 12, 18, 24]:
    rs, ru = _nearest(ds_s, "age_months", a), _nearest(ds_u, "age_months", a)
    rows.append({
        "Age (mo)": a,
        "Spoken σ_Y TD": f"{rs['sdY_TD_median']:.0f}",
        "Spoken σ_Y DS": f"{rs['sdY_DS_median']:.0f}",
        "Spoken φ TD/DS": f"{rs['phi_ratio_median']:.2f}",
        "Understood σ_Y TD": f"{ru['sdY_TD_median']:.0f}",
        "Understood σ_Y DS": f"{ru['sdY_DS_median']:.0f}",
        "Understood φ TD/DS": f"{ru['phi_ratio_median']:.2f}",
    })
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Age (mo)")
```

Two distinct stories:

- **Comprehension:** the overdispersion factor is comparable across groups at all
  ages (φ_TD/φ_DS ≈ 1) — the residual the Beta-Binomial layer carries is of similar
  relative size in both. TD's larger _absolute_ spread σ_Y is essentially a
  consequence of its larger mean.
- **Production:** early DS spoken counts are slightly _more_ overdispersed than TD
  (φ_TD/φ_DS < 1 in the first months), but the ordering **reverses during the
  second year**: as TD production explodes its absolute spread balloons (σ_Y ~5 →
  ~70+ words by ~18 mo) while DS production stays compressed near the floor, and
  TD becomes the more overdispersed group. DS production is not just lower — it is
  also far less variable in absolute terms across the overlap.

Read the second bullet with the floor in mind. At 8 months almost every TD child
produces no words at all, so TD counts are near-Binomial there and φ is close to
its lower limit; that is a floor, not a population of unusually similar children.
The same mechanism compresses DS production across the whole overlap window.

![Between-child spread σ_Y — spoken](ds_td_spoken_re_spread.png){#fig-sd-s .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![Residual overdispersion φ (study + subject REs) — spoken](ds_td_spoken_re_overdispersion.png){#fig-phi-s .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![Between-child spread σ_Y — understood](ds_td_understood_re_spread.png){#fig-sd-u .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![Residual overdispersion φ (study + subject REs) — understood](ds_td_understood_re_overdispersion.png){#fig-phi-u .lightbox fig-align="left"}

## Between-child heterogeneity {#sec-between-child}

The contrast the previous section cannot make. $\tau$ is the SD, across children of
the same age, of the child's own logit for this outcome — the population-relative
measure of how much children differ — and $\sigma_{child}$ is the spread in
expected words it induces, which is what a clinician would see. $\sigma_{child}$
counts only persistent between-child differences: unlike $\sigma_Y$ it excludes
the Beta-Binomial noise.

$\tau$ is a parameter on the TD side (`tau_subject`, constant in age) but a
*derived* quantity on the DS side. VG20 places its child effects on understood
(`tau_subj_u`) and on the production ratio (`tau_subj_q`), with spoken built as
$p_S = p_U \cdot q$, so it has no spoken child scale to read off, and the induced
spoken $\tau$ varies with age even though both underlying scales are constants.
Contrasting `tau_subj_q` against `tau_subject` directly would set the spread of a
*conversion ratio* against the spread of a *level*; the derivation in
`comparison.subject_heterogeneity` avoids that.

```{python}
he_s = pd.read_csv("ds_td_spoken_re_subject_heterogeneity.csv")
he_u = pd.read_csv("ds_td_understood_re_subject_heterogeneity.csv")
rows = []
for a in [8, 12, 18, 24]:
    rs, ru = _nearest(he_s, "age_months", a), _nearest(he_u, "age_months", a)
    rows.append({
        "Age (mo)": a,
        "Spoken τ TD": f"{rs['tau_TD_median']:.2f}",
        "Spoken τ DS": f"{rs['tau_DS_median']:.2f}",
        "Spoken τ TD/DS": f"{rs['tau_ratio_median']:.2f}",
        "Spoken σ_child TD": f"{rs['sdchild_TD_median']:.0f}",
        "Spoken σ_child DS": f"{rs['sdchild_DS_median']:.0f}",
        "Understood τ TD": f"{ru['tau_TD_median']:.2f}",
        "Understood τ DS": f"{ru['tau_DS_median']:.2f}",
        "Understood τ TD/DS": f"{ru['tau_ratio_median']:.2f}",
    })
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Age (mo)")
```

![Between-child heterogeneity τ — spoken](ds_td_spoken_re_subject_tau.png){#fig-tau-s .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![Between-child spread in expected words σ_child — spoken](ds_td_spoken_re_subject_spread.png){#fig-sdc-s .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![Between-child heterogeneity τ — understood](ds_td_understood_re_subject_tau.png){#fig-tau-u .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![Between-child spread in expected words σ_child — understood](ds_td_understood_re_subject_spread.png){#fig-sdc-u .lightbox fig-align="left"}

**The two scales disagree, and the relative one reverses the absolute reading.**
Children with Down syndrome differ from one another _more_ than typically developing children do, on both outcomes and at every age in the overlap, with posterior probability ≈ 1.00.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
# Computed, not typed: an earlier hand-written version of this paragraph quoted
# spoken τ_DS as "1.44 at 8 months to 1.27 at 30" and the ratio as "0.72 rising
# to 0.82". Under the 13-16 August refits that became 1.47 → 1.31 and 0.70 →
# 0.80; under VG20's correlated between-child derivation (2026-08-19) it is

_lo, _hi = float(he_s["age_months"].min()), float(he_s["age_months"].max())
_a, _b = _nearest(he_s, "age_months", _lo), _nearest(he_s, "age_months", _hi)
_u = _nearest(he_u, "age_months", he_u["age_months"].max())
_ulo, _uhi = float(he_u["age_months"].min()), float(he_u["age_months"].max())
_sd = _nearest(he_s, "age_months", _hi)
print(
    f"For spoken words τ_DS runs {_a['tau_DS_median']:.2f} at {_lo:.0f} months to "
    f"{_b['tau_DS_median']:.2f} at {_hi:.0f}, against a constant τ_TD of "
    f"{_a['tau_TD_median']:.2f} (ratio {_a['tau_ratio_median']:.2f} rising to "
    f"{_b['tau_ratio_median']:.2f}); for comprehension, over its own narrower "
    f"overlap of {_ulo:.0f}–{_uhi:.0f} months, τ_DS is {_u['tau_DS_median']:.2f} "
    f"against τ_TD {_u['tau_TD_median']:.2f} (ratio {_u['tau_ratio_median']:.2f}). "
    f"Because only the DS side varies with age, a single ratio has to be quoted "
    f"with the age it is read at. Yet σ_child in words runs the other way by a "
    f"wide margin — {_sd['sdchild_TD_median']:.0f} words TD against "
    f"{_sd['sdchild_DS_median']:.0f} DS for spoken at {_hi:.0f} months — because "
    f"the typically developing group sits at a far higher level, and the same "
    f"relative spread around a larger mean is a larger absolute spread."
)
```

Both statements describe the same posterior. Which one answers "are these children more alike?" depends on what is being asked: on the population-relative scale Down syndrome vocabulary is the _more_ variable of the two, while in absolute word counts it is much the less variable. Neither is the reading a glance at the overdispersion panel above would suggest, which is the point of separating the two sections.

The age profiles differ by construction, and are worth reading as a check on the derivation. τ_TD is flat because the univariate models place a single intercept on the outcome's logit; τ_DS for comprehension is flat for the same reason. τ_DS for _spoken_ declines with age even though both of VG20's subject scales are constants, because the spoken logit is reached through $p_U$ and $q$ — that decline is a property of the product form, not a finding about children becoming more alike.

::: {.callout-important title="The spoken contrast carries an assumption the comprehension contrast does not"}
The comprehension contrast is like-for-like in a strong sense: a single Gaussian intercept on the understood logit on both sides. The spoken contrast is not, in three ways, and only the third biases the number.

**Induced versus primitive.** τ_TD is a free parameter; τ_DS is derived by integrating $\text{sigmoid}(f_u + \tau_u Z_1)\cdot\text{sigmoid}(h + \tau_q Z_2)$. Targeting the SD of the child's *spoken logit* is what makes the two the same estimand — the alternative, contrasting `tau_subj_q` against `tau_subject`, would set the spread of a conversion ratio against the spread of a level. But the induced child-logit distribution is skewed where the TD one is exactly Gaussian, so equal τ matches the first two moments of differently shaped distributions and does not imply equal spread in the tails.

**Age.** Only the DS side varies with age, so the ratio is a curve read at a point, not a single contrast.

**An independence constraint that used to sit on one side only — now removed.** VG10 drew each child's comprehension deviation and production-ratio deviation as two independent standard Normals, estimated no correlation between them, and the derivation above assumed that independence; VG11's single spoken intercept never placed such a restriction, absorbing the whole between-child spoken variance, correlation included. So the asymmetry was in the contrast, not in one model's internals. **VG20 estimates the correlation**, and since 2026-08-19 the derivation above integrates $Z_2 = \rho Z_1 + \sqrt{1-\rho^2}\,Z_2'$ rather than an independent $Z_2$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
_c = pd.read_csv("ds_subject_effect_correlation.csv")
_c = _c.assign(_k=_c["model"].str.lower()).set_index("_k")
_now = _c.loc["vg20"] if "vg20" in _c.index else _c.iloc[0]
_then = _c.loc["vg10"] if "vg10" in _c.index else None
_txt = (
    f"The fitted correlation is **+0.368** (89% interval +0.287 to +0.447); read "
    f"back out of the model's own per-child deviations it is "
    f"{_now['corr_median']:+.3f} ({_now['corr_ci_lo']:+.3f} to "
    f"{_now['corr_ci_hi']:+.3f}) across {_now['n_children']:.0f} children, which is "
    f"the check that the parameter does what it claims to."
)
if _then is not None:
    _txt += (
        f" The superseded model's deviations correlated at only "
        f"{_then['corr_median']:+.3f} ({_then['corr_ci_lo']:+.3f} to "
        f"{_then['corr_ci_hi']:+.3f}) — the difference is the pull of a prior that "
        f"asserted independence, not a difference between the children."
    )
_txt += (
    " Since $\\log p_S = \\log p_U + \\log q$ gains $2\\,\\mathrm{Cov}$, the "
    "independent-draw derivation **understated** the DS spoken between-child scale "
    "by about 15% on the logit scale at every age. τ_DS for comprehension is "
    "unaffected, as it must be: the correlation changes how the two deviations "
    "co-vary, not either one's marginal spread."
)
print(_txt)
```

The direction is what saved the earlier finding. DS was already the more variable side, so the correction moves the spoken ratio further below 1 — it strengthens rather than reverses, and the tables above now carry the corrected value. Every spoken between-child contrast published before 2026-08-19 is superseded by this and was biased toward the comprehension value; the comprehension contrast is unchanged, and the two rows can now be read against each other, which the bias did not previously permit.

One caveat survives, pointing the other way. 432 of the 767 children are seen once, and 342 of those inform the correlation only through the agreement between two counts on a single questionnaire completed by one parent — where shared reporter bias is not separable from shared child ability. So **+0.368 leans high**. VG16's cross-lag, which reads the child's comprehension from a *different* administration and is therefore immune to that artefact, implies about **+0.24** (89% interval +0.11 to +0.38) once corrected for the unreliability of its predictor. The two overlap; the truth is more likely in the lower half of VG20's interval, which would put the correction at somewhat less than the 15% quoted above.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="And the comprehension contrast carries a measured bias the spoken one does not"}
The section above calls the comprehension contrast the like-for-like one, and structurally it is. But structural symmetry is not the same as an unbiased estimate, and parameter recovery finds the bias on this side rather than the other.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
import glob
_rr = [
    pd.read_csv(f)
    for f in sorted(glob.glob("recovery_vg12_r*.csv"))
    if "aggregates" not in f
]
_ts = pd.concat([d[d["quantity"] == "tau_subject"] for d in _rr])
_sh = pd.concat([d[d["quantity"] == "subject_variance_share"] for d in _rr])
_vt = pd.concat([d[d["quantity"] == "v_total"] for d in _rr])
_miss = int((~_ts["within_ci89"]).sum())
_bias = float((_ts["posterior_mean"] / _ts["truth"] - 1.0).mean())
_zs = ", ".join(f"{z:+.2f}" for z in _ts["z"])
print(
    f"Refitting VG12 to data simulated from its own posterior returns "
    f"`tau_subject` below the truth in {len(_ts)} replicates of {len(_ts)} "
    f"(z = {_zs}), a bias of {_bias:+.1%}, with the truth outside the 89% "
    f"interval {_miss} of {len(_ts)} times. The budget is not what is "
    f"mis-estimated — `v_total` recovers with z = "
    f"{', '.join(f'{z:+.2f}' for z in _vt['z'])} — but the split is, with "
    f"`subject_variance_share` low at z = "
    f"{', '.join(f'{z:+.2f}' for z in _sh['z'])}. "
    f"$\\tau_{{subject}} = \\sqrt{{share \\cdot v_{{total}}}}$ inherits that "
    f"amplified, because the transformation concentrates its posterior."
)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
_r0 = he_u.iloc[0]
_corr = (_r0["tau_TD_median"] / (1.0 + _bias)) / _r0["tau_DS_median"]
_word = "overstates" if _corr > _r0["tau_ratio_median"] else "understates"
print(
    f"$\\tau_{{subject}}$ is the typically-developing side of this contrast, so "
    f"a low bias there **{_word}** the reported difference: the ratio TD/DS of "
    f"{_r0['tau_ratio_median']:.3f} would sit near {_corr:.2f} if the bias "
    f"carried over at the size these replicates suggest. The direction is "
    f"opposite to the independence bias on the spoken side above, so the two "
    f"outcomes are biased *toward each other* — which inflates any reading of "
    f"the comprehension and spoken ratios against one another at both ends."
)
```

Three `test`-tier replicates, truths drawn from the model's own posterior, so this is a self-consistency check and the magnitude should not be quoted. The direction is consistent and has a mechanism. VG11 carries the same reparameterisation at a very different reference proportion and has not been through recovery. Tracked as issue #225; the evidence is in `notes/202608161700-recovery-baseline-215.md`.
:::

Two further caveats bound how far this contrast can be pushed. First, the priors
are not symmetric: on the TD side $\tau_{subject}$ and $\kappa$ are sampled
through the shared-budget reparameterisation, with an informative prior on how
the budget splits, while on the DS side they are two free scales — so part of any
$\tau$ difference is a difference in prior structure, and the TD pool averages
1.21 observations per child, which is what made that reparameterisation necessary
in the first place. Second, $\tau$ is matched on *age*. At matched age the DS group
sits near a floor where any spread measure is mechanically small, so a like-for-like
reading of "are these children more alike" also wants the comparison at matched
vocabulary level — which is what the attainment-delay and matched-comprehension
sections provide.

## Sign-inclusive expressive gap

```{python}
si = pd.read_csv("ds_td_sign_inclusive.csv")
rows = []
for a in [16, 20, 24, 30]:
    r = _nearest(si, "age_months", a)
    gap_sp = r["gap_spoken_median"]
    gap_any = r["gap_any_median"]
    gap_indep = r["gap_any_indep_median"]
    narrow = (gap_sp - gap_any) / gap_sp if gap_sp else float("nan")
    narrow_indep = (gap_sp - gap_indep) / gap_sp if gap_sp else float("nan")
    rows.append({
        "Age (mo)": a,
        "Sign credit (words)": band_at(si, "age_months", a, "credit", dec=0),
        "Gap (spoken only)": f"{gap_sp:.0f}",
        "Gap (with sign)": f"{gap_any:.0f}",
        "Narrowed by": f"{narrow:.0%}",
        "…if independence assumed": f"{narrow_indep:.0%}",
    })
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Age (mo)")
```

Counting signed words (DS total expressive `p_any` from VG15) credits DS extra
early expressive vocabulary and narrows the DS–TD expressive gap by ~11–13% in
the 24–30 mo window, and by more at younger ages where TD production is still
small. Real, but modest **against this comparator**: the gap stays enormous
because TD production is mid-explosion here. Read this alongside
@sec-ds-signing, which asks what signing is worth to the child rather than to the
gap, and reaches a very different-looking number from the same posterior.

The last column is the same contrast computed **as if** sign and speech were
independent given age. VG15 measures that association at $\psi$ = 2.34
(89% ETI [1.89, 2.81], P($\psi$>1) = 1.00) — a child who signs a word is more
likely to also say it — so independence double-counts the overlap and overstates
total expressive vocabulary. The overstatement is small here (under one
percentage point of narrowing, 1.6 words at 24 mo), but it is reported rather
than assumed away, and it is why this section reads VG15 rather than the
independence-assuming VG14.

::: {.callout-warning title="Two bounds on this contrast"}
**The window is capped at 30 months by TD support, not by signing data.** DS
signing is now observed on 904 administrations from 549 children across nine
studies, out to 115 months. Every observation above 30 months — including all of
`uk_07`'s and `uk_06`'s — is outside this figure and cannot enter it. No amount
of further DS signing data will extend this section; @sec-ds-signing is where
that evidence goes.

**TD expressive vocabulary is assumed to equal TD spoken vocabulary.** The
Wordbank source carries comprehension and production only, with no gesture or
sign measure, so TD receives a sign credit of exactly zero by construction rather
than by measurement. For lexical signing that is a reasonable assumption — TD
children are not generally taught a sign vocabulary — but it is an assumption,
and it works in the direction of making the narrowing look larger.
:::

![DS expressive gap to TD: spoken-only vs sign-inclusive](ds_td_sign_inclusive_gap.png){#fig-si-gap .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![DS expressive credit from non-speech modalities](ds_td_sign_inclusive_credit.png){#fig-si-credit .lightbox fig-align="left"}

## What signing is worth to the child {#sec-ds-signing}

The section above measures signing against typically developing children, where
it looks marginal. That is the wrong denominator for a parent, a teacher or a
speech and language therapist, and it is bounded at 30 months by a comparator
this question does not need. Dropping the comparator changes both: the DS-internal
quantities run to the comprehension reporting cap at 72 months, and the effect
stops looking marginal.

```{python}
sp = pd.read_csv("ds_signing_profile.csv")
rows = []
for a in [18, 24, 30, 36, 48, 60, 72]:
    r = _nearest(sp, "age_months", a)
    rows.append({
        "Age (mo)": a,
        "Spoken": f"{r['spoken_median']:.0f}",
        "Any modality": f"{r['any_median']:.0f}",
        "× spoken alone": band_at(sp, "age_months", a, "uplift", dec=2),
        "Sign-only words": f"{r['sign_only_median']:.0f}",
        "Share sign-only": band_at(sp, "age_months", a, "sign_only_share", dec=2),
    })
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Age (mo)")
```

At two years a child with Down syndrome expresses about **four times** as much
vocabulary as a speech-only count records, and roughly **three-quarters of
everything they can express is available only in sign**. A speech-only assessment
at that age is not measuring a slightly smaller vocabulary — it is missing most
of it.

The uplift then falls away steadily: ×2.2 at 36 months, ×1.3 at 48, ×1.06 by 72.
**This is signing as a bridge** — it carries the most weight exactly where speech
is least available, and hands over as speech arrives — and the hand-over has
identifiable milestones:

```{python}
ms = pd.read_csv("ds_signing_milestones.csv").set_index("quantity")
labels = {
    "sign_only_peak_age": "Sign-only vocabulary peaks (mo)",
    "sign_only_peak_words": "…at how many words",
    "sign_only_share_below_half_age": "Sign-only falls below half of expressive vocabulary (mo)",
    "speech_only_overtakes_sign_only_age": "Speech-only overtakes sign-only (mo)",
}
pd.DataFrame([
    {"Milestone": lab,
     "Estimate": _hdi(ms.loc[k, "median"], ms.loc[k, "ci_lo"], ms.loc[k, "ci_hi"], 1),
     "Draws reaching it": f"{ms.loc[k, 'draws_reaching']:.0%}",
     **({"Draws censored": f"{ms.loc[k, 'draws_censored']:.0%}"}
        if "draws_censored" in ms.columns else {})}
    for k, lab in labels.items()
]).set_index("Milestone")
```

The `Draws reaching it` column is the identification check: a crossing counts
only when the state genuinely flips inside the grid (a state already true at the
youngest established age is censored, not an early crossing, and a peak on a
grid edge is censored rather than located). Read a milestone reached in less
than all draws as a bound rather than an estimate.

The three arrive in that order, and the spacing is the substantive part.
Sign-only vocabulary stops *growing* at ≈34 months, but it is still the majority
of everything the child can express for another ≈4 months, and still larger than
speech-only for ≈5 months beyond that. So the two crossings are not signing
falling away — they happen on a slow decline from about 50 words to about 44,
while speech-only nearly triples over the same span (17 → 45). **Signing is overtaken
because speech grows, not because signing stops.**

The signed fraction of comprehension $r(a)$ tells the same story on its own
scale, peaking near 29 months at 0.33 and falling to 0.15 by 84. Note that it
peaks *earlier* than the sign-only word count above, and so does the sign-only
share of comprehension (≈28 months) — no contradiction, because those are
**shares** and this is a **count**. Sign-only words are understood words × the
sign-only share, so their growth rates add; at 28 months comprehension is still
growing at ~6% a month while the share is flat, so the count keeps rising until
the share's decline is steep enough to cancel it at ~34 months. The gap is a
statement about comprehension still growing, not about signing. VG15's report
works this through.

Nothing here says the bridge *causes* the crossing — see the caveat below — but
the shape of the hand-over is now measurable, which it was not before `uk_07` and
the reinstated `uk_06` signing rows extended the signed tail past 30 months.

![How DS expressive vocabulary is expressed](ds_signing_composition.png){#fig-ds-sign-comp .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![Signing as a bridge: its share falls as speech arrives](ds_signing_share.png){#fig-ds-sign-share .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![What counting sign adds to a child's own expressive vocabulary](ds_signing_uplift.png){#fig-ds-sign-uplift .lightbox fig-align="left"}

::: {.callout-important title="Does early signing predict later speech?"}
The obvious follow-up — do children who sign more go on to *say* more? — is
answerable in these data only in part, and
[`notes/202608160930`](https://github.com/dseinternational/vocabulary-growth/blob/main/notes/202608160930-early-signing-and-later-speech.md)
records the attempt. Among 147 children with signing, comprehension and speech at
an early wave and speech at a later one, and holding the child's earlier speech
and comprehension standing fixed, **how much** a child signs relative to what they
understand predicts later spoken vocabulary (+0.19 SD per SD, 89% ETI
[0.03, 0.36], stable under study fixed effects and under dropping any single
study). **Whether** a child signs at all does not separate: that contrast spans
zero and flips sign when any one study is dropped, because signing is very nearly
a study-level property here — two studies are ~100% signers and one is 0%.

None of this is causal. Signing is taught *because* a child is not talking, so the
residual selection pushes the estimate down, which is the one direction that
helps: a positive association survives that bias. It is not evidence that teaching
signs raises speech.
:::

## Reading

DS early vocabulary is best described as a **developmental stretch with a
production-specific deficit**: comprehension is delayed and the delay widens with
level; production is delayed _substantially more_ (~12–17 extra months at matched
low vocabulary size, P > 0 ≈ 1.00), peaks several years later, and leaves ~90% of
2-year-old children below the TD 10th centile for spoken words. Residual
Beta-Binomial dispersion is comparable for comprehension, while DS production
stays compressed near the floor across the overlap; how much children within each
population differ from one another is a separate question, answered by $\tau$ in
@sec-between-child rather than by anything in the dispersion section.

Signing compensates partially — and how partial depends entirely on the
denominator, which is the one place in this report where the same posterior
supports two honest headlines that sound opposed. Against typically developing
children it closes ~11–13% of the expressive gap at 24–30 months: real, modest,
and bounded at 30 months by the comparator. Against the child's own repertoire it
is the difference between saying 9 words and expressing 37 at two years, with
three-quarters of that available only in sign. Both are true. The first is the
right number for describing the population gap; the second is the right number
for deciding how to assess a two-year-old, and it is the one the earlier drafts
of this report did not carry.

Every headline here is recovered from the disjoint fits with exact intervals,
with no joint model required.
